newsitem.title: NICARAGUA: Polarized Nicaraguans to vote for president.
newsitem.headline: Polarized Nicaraguans to vote for president.

text.p: Nicaraguans vote for president on Sunday in a passionate, polarised election that pits a right-wing populist against the Sandinista ruler who led the country through revolution and war in the 1980s.
The battle fought at the ballot box parallels the struggle that has wrenched Nicaragua for much of this century.

The two leading candidates are Arnoldo Aleman of the Liberal Alliance, whose backers include exiles once firmly allied to a right-wing dictatorship, and Daniel Ortega, who led Nicaragua's Marxist revolutionary government from 1979-1990.
Polls were due to open at 7 a.m. local time (1300 GMT) and electoral authorities were expecting a huge, peaceful turnout from the 2.4 million registered voters.
A daunting 23 candidates were on the presidential ballot, most of them from centrist parties only expected to muster a small portion of the vote.

In Nicaragua, whose recent history is a bloody saga of dictatorship, civil war and U.S. involvement, voters follow politics with a passion that only baseball can rival. The close contest has all the hallmarks of a ninth-inning showdown.

The final CID-Gallup poll last week measured Aleman's support at 40.5 percent, his once-mighty lead narrowed to 2.6 percentage points over Ortega. If neither candidate achieves 45 percent on Sunday, the election goes to a second round.
Analysts say the deciding factor in a race that has been dominated by two old-style political strongmen is the allegiance of the nation's poor.

In the most underdeveloped country in Latin America after Haiti, where unemployment runs at 54 percent, both have pledged jobs, economic recovery and strong leadership after the rudderless six-year rule of President Violeta Chamorro.

"The immense majority of the poor that today are without hope will be the major deciders of this contest," wrote the president's son, independent political analyst Carlos Fernando Chamorro, in his Confidencial newsletter on Sunday.
"Probably their expectations of the solutions a new government offers are exaggerated, but no one can blame them for having faith in the future," he wrote.
Courting undecided voters, both Aleman and Ortega have dredged up the other's past to suggest that a vote cast against them would be a step back toward dictatorship.
Both, meanwhile, have sought to paint themselves as modern, business-friendly moderates with development and reconciliation at the top of their agendas.

Ortega, who led Nicaragua through an eight-year war with U.S.-backed Contra rebels in which 25,000 people died, has made a stunning conversion from revolutionary "Commandante" in military fatigues to neatly-dressed social democrat offering the hand of friendship to Washington.
Many Nicaraguans mistrust the transition, but the United States has assured voters it will respect the vote whichever way it goes.
"We're not taking sides in this election. We can accept whoever the Nicaraguan people select," Brian Atwood, President Bill Clinton's envoy to the elections, said late on Saturday.

Aleman, a burly former mayor of Managua who was once a prisoner of Ortega's government, has raised tensions among his opponents by demanding that powerful Sandinistas pay for the state-owned properties they seized before leaving office.

He has also refused to denounce former dictator Anastasio Somoza, saying the Sandinistas that toppled him are a greater evil. That stance, a bone thrown to his hard-right backers, has cost him votes at the political centre, analysts say.

On the ballot nationwide will be a staggering 32,000 candidates. Besides the presidential contenders will be those for vice-president, 145 mayors and 145 councilors, 90 federal deputies and 20 members of the Central American parliament.
Polls were due to close at 6 p.m. (midnight GMT), but first results were not expected until early Monday.
